cards.subject: Continuous integration
says: merges every developer's changes into a shared branch frequently
builds and tests each change automatically as it lands
cards.use: want integration problems found within minutes of a commit
not: ships each change to customers without running any tests

cards.subject: Continuous delivery
says: keeps every passing change in a releasable state
leaves the decision to release to production to a person
cards.use: want to be able to ship any green build on demand but choose when
not: pushes every commit to production with no human decision

cards.subject: Continuous deployment
says: releases every change that passes the pipeline to production automatically
has no manual approval step before production
cards.use: trust your automated checks enough to ship each green commit without a gate
not: requires a person to click release for every change

cards.subject: A build artifact
says: is the single versioned output of a build that later stages deploy
can be stored and identified by a version number or hash
cards.use: need a stored, versioned build output that any stage can fetch
not: is rebuilt from source from scratch in every environment

cards.subject: A dependency lockfile
says: records the exact resolved version of every dependency
makes an install on another machine reproduce the same dependency tree
cards.use: need a repeatable install on a clean server
not: lets each machine pick the newest version on every install

cards.subject: A quality gate
says: blocks promotion to the next stage when a defined check fails
turns a policy such as test results or scan findings into a pass or fail decision
cards.use: need a release stopped automatically when a required check fails
not: only logs a warning and always lets the release continue

cards.subject: Fail fast
says: stops the pipeline at the first failing step
puts the cheapest and quickest checks first
cards.use: want developers to learn about a broken build in seconds rather than after the full run
not: runs every remaining step after a failure to collect all results

cards.subject: Pipeline as code
says: defines the pipeline in a versioned file next to the source
makes pipeline changes reviewable like any other change
cards.use: want pipeline changes to go through code review and be revertable
not: is configured only in a web console that keeps no history

cards.subject: A build cache
says: reuses unchanged work from earlier runs to shorten builds
can serve stale output when its key leaves out an input
cards.use: want faster builds when most inputs have not changed
not: guarantees a correct build even when an input is missing from its key

cards.subject: Job parallelism
says: runs independent jobs at the same time to shorten total pipeline time
is limited by jobs that depend on each other's output
cards.use: want a long test suite split across several runners
not: lets a deploy job start before the build it needs has finished

cards.subject: Promotion between environments
says: moves the same tested artifact from one environment to the next
happens only after the checks of the earlier environment pass
cards.use: need staging and production to run exactly the same bits
not: rebuilds the code for each environment so each gets a fresh build

cards.subject: A unit test
says: checks one small piece of code in isolation
runs in milliseconds with collaborators replaced by fakes
cards.use: want instant feedback on one function's logic
not: needs a full deployed environment and a real database

cards.subject: An integration test
says: checks that several components work together, such as code and a real database
fails when two parts disagree about an interface
cards.use: need to verify the app's code against a real database or service
not: isolates each function from every collaborator using fakes

cards.subject: An end-to-end test
says: drives the whole application through its user interface like a user
covers a full journey across every layer
cards.use: need to prove a complete journey such as log in and check out still works
not: is the fastest and most stable kind of automated test

cards.subject: A smoke test
says: runs a few fast checks that a fresh deploy is basically alive
verifies the app responds rather than that every feature is correct
cards.use: want a quick check right after a deploy
not: replaces the full regression suite

cards.subject: A regression test
says: guards against a previously fixed bug returning
is usually added at the moment a bug is fixed
cards.use: just fixed a bug and want to be sure it never comes back
not: is written only before any code exists

cards.subject: A contract test
says: checks that a service and its consumer agree on the shape of requests and responses
lets two teams change independently while catching breaking API changes
cards.use: need to catch an API change that would break a consumer without running both systems together
not: measures how the service behaves under heavy traffic

cards.subject: A load test
says: measures behavior under expected or peak traffic
reveals throughput limits and latency growth under concurrency
cards.use: need to know how much traffic the service handles before it slows down
not: checks that a single function returns the right value

cards.subject: A soak test
says: runs sustained load for hours to expose slow leaks
finds memory growth that short tests miss
cards.use: suspect a memory leak that only shows after hours of running
not: finds the maximum throughput in a one-minute burst

cards.subject: The development environment
says: is where a developer runs and changes the app locally
uses local configuration and throwaway data
cards.use: are writing and trying code on your own machine
not: serves real customers and holds their data

cards.subject: The staging environment
says: mirrors production closely to rehearse a release
is where a release candidate gets its final checks
cards.use: want to rehearse a release on production-like infrastructure before real users see it
not: holds the live customer data

cards.subject: The production environment
says: serves real users and holds real data
must never share secrets or databases with other environments
cards.use: need the live service that customers depend on
not: is the right place to try out risky experiments first

cards.subject: A sandbox environment
says: is a safe place to experiment where actions have no real-world effect
stubs or blocks outbound effects such as real email
cards.use: want to try a risky integration without contacting real people or moving real money
not: sends real email to real customers so tests feel realistic

cards.subject: A preview environment
says: is a short-lived copy created for one pull request
is torn down when the pull request closes
cards.use: want reviewers to click through a change before it merges
not: is the long-lived shared copy used for final release checks

cards.subject: Environment parity
says: keeps development, staging and production as similar as practical
makes surprises appear early instead of in production
cards.use: keep finding bugs that only appear in production
not: requires production to be a scaled-down copy of development

cards.subject: An environment variable
says: supplies configuration to a process from outside the code
lets the same build behave differently in each environment
cards.use: need the same code to use a different database path or API key per environment
not: is the right place to commit a production password to the repository

cards.subject: Test data
says: should be synthetic or anonymised rather than raw production records
keeps personal data out of non-production environments
cards.use: need realistic records in staging without exposing customers' information
not: is best copied unchanged from production

cards.subject: A feature branch
says: isolates one piece of work until it is ready to merge
is normally short-lived and deleted after merging
cards.use: want to work on a change without disturbing the main line
not: has to stay open until the next scheduled release

cards.subject: Trunk-based development
says: has everyone integrate small changes into one main branch at least daily
relies on feature flags to hide unfinished work
cards.use: want to avoid long-lived branches and painful merges
not: requires a long-lived develop branch alongside main

cards.subject: GitFlow
says: uses long-lived main and develop branches plus release and hotfix branches
suits software shipped in scheduled, versioned releases
cards.use: ship versioned releases on a schedule and must maintain more than one version
not: merges straight to main many times a day with no other long-lived branches

cards.subject: GitHub Flow
says: branches from main, opens a pull request and merges back to main
treats main as always deployable
cards.use: deploy continuously from main with review through pull requests
not: keeps a permanent develop branch that collects work before release

cards.subject: A release branch
says: is cut from main to stabilise one particular version
receives only fixes while main moves on
cards.use: need to harden version 2.4 while new work continues on main
not: is where every new feature is developed first

cards.subject: A hotfix
says: ships an urgent fix to production outside the normal release cycle
must be merged back so later releases keep the fix
cards.use: find production broken and cannot wait for the next scheduled release
not: waits in the queue for the next planned release like any other change

cards.subject: Semantic versioning
says: numbers releases as major.minor.patch
bumps the major number for backwards-incompatible changes
cards.use: need version numbers that tell consumers whether an upgrade can break them
not: bumps the patch number whenever a new feature is added

cards.subject: A release tag
says: marks the exact commit a release was built from
lets you rebuild or inspect a past release
cards.use: need to find exactly what code is running as version 1.8.2
not: moves automatically to the newest commit on main

cards.subject: A merge queue
says: tests each pull request against the latest main plus the changes queued ahead of it
stops two individually green changes from breaking main together
cards.use: want main to stay green when many pull requests merge at once
not: merges pull requests in random order without re-testing them

cards.subject: A rolling deployment
says: replaces instances a few at a time with the new version
keeps some capacity serving throughout without a second full environment
cards.use: want zero downtime without paying for a duplicate environment
not: switches all traffic at once to a second identical environment

cards.subject: A blue/green deployment
says: runs two identical environments and switches traffic from the old to the new
makes rollback a switch back to the previous environment
cards.use: need an instant cutover and an instant way back
not: updates instances one by one in place

cards.subject: A canary release
says: sends a small share of real traffic to the new version first
expands only if the metrics for that small share stay healthy
cards.use: want to limit the damage of a bad release to a few users
not: switches every user to the new version at the same moment

cards.subject: A recreate deployment
says: stops the old version completely before starting the new one
causes a short downtime window
cards.use: can accept a brief outage and want the simplest possible deploy
not: keeps old and new versions serving side by side during the change

cards.subject: A feature flag
says: turns a code path on or off at runtime without a deploy
separates deploying code from releasing a feature
cards.use: want to ship unfinished code safely and switch it on later or for a few users
not: requires a new build to change its value

cards.subject: Shadow traffic
says: copies live requests to the new version and discards its responses
tests a new version against real traffic with no user impact
cards.use: want to compare a rewrite against real traffic before any user depends on it
not: returns the new version's responses to a small share of users

cards.subject: A rollback
says: returns production to the previous known-good version
is fastest when the previous artifact is still available
cards.use: see a release failing and need service restored within minutes
not: requires building the previous version from source again

cards.subject: A roll forward
says: fixes a bad release by shipping a new corrected version
is often the safer choice after an irreversible data migration
cards.use: face a bad release that already changed data in a way the old version cannot read
not: restores the previous version by redeploying it unchanged

cards.subject: An expand and contract migration
says: adds the new schema first, moves the code over, then removes the old schema
lets old and new versions of the app run against the same database
cards.use: need a schema change with zero downtime during a rolling deploy
not: drops the old column in the same release that stops using it

cards.subject: Progressive delivery
says: widens exposure in stages guided by live metrics
combines canaries and flags with automated promotion or abort
cards.use: want a rollout that advances or aborts by itself based on the error rate
not: releases to everyone first and measures afterwards

cards.subject: A container
says: packages an app with its dependencies so it runs the same anywhere
shares the host's kernel rather than booting a full operating system
cards.use: need an app to run identically on a laptop and a server
not: boots its own complete kernel like a virtual machine

cards.subject: A container image
says: is the read-only template a container is started from
is built in layers from instructions such as a Dockerfile
cards.use: need a versioned, shareable package to start many identical containers
not: holds the changing state of a running container

cards.subject: A volume
says: keeps data outside the container's disposable filesystem
survives the container being deleted and recreated
cards.use: run a database in a container and must not lose its data on redeploy
not: is wiped each time the container restarts

cards.subject: A process manager
says: starts an app, restarts it after a crash and brings it back after a reboot
keeps an app alive without someone watching it
cards.use: need a Node server to come back by itself after it dies
not: builds the app from source before every start

cards.subject: A reverse proxy
says: accepts client requests and forwards them to an app behind it
can terminate TLS and hide the app's real port
cards.use: want one public front door such as Apache or Nginx in front of an app on a private port
not: is the origin application that generates the pages

cards.subject: Binding to localhost
says: makes a service listen only on 127.0.0.1
keeps a port unreachable from other machines
cards.use: want an internal service reachable only by a reverse proxy on the same machine
not: makes the service reachable from the whole internet

cards.subject: A resource limit
says: caps the memory or CPU a process or container may use
stops one runaway process starving its neighbours
cards.use: want a memory leak to hurt one process rather than the whole host
not: lets a process use unlimited memory when it needs it

cards.subject: Graceful shutdown
says: lets a process finish in-flight requests before it exits on a termination signal
prevents dropped requests during a restart
cards.use: restart a server during a deploy without cutting users off mid-request
not: kills the process instantly so no work is left half done

cards.subject: A liveness check
says: tells the platform whether a process is stuck and needs restarting
should not fail merely because a downstream dependency is down
cards.use: need a hung process to be killed and restarted automatically
not: keeps an instance out of rotation while it starts up

cards.subject: A readiness check
says: tells the load balancer whether an instance can accept traffic yet
keeps an instance out of rotation while it starts up or warms its caches
cards.use: want traffic held back until the app has finished starting
not: restarts the process whenever it fails

cards.subject: A container orchestrator
says: schedules containers across several machines and restarts failed ones
reconciles the running state to a declared desired state
cards.use: run many containers across several hosts and want failures healed automatically
not: is a library for writing unit tests

cards.subject: Infrastructure as code
says: describes servers, networks and services in versioned files
lets infrastructure changes be reviewed and repeated
cards.use: want to rebuild an environment from a repository instead of from memory
not: means clicking through a console and writing down what you did

cards.subject: Declarative configuration
says: states the desired end result and lets the tool work out the steps
can be applied repeatedly to converge on the same state
cards.use: want to say three servers with this setup and have a tool make it so
not: lists every command to run in order

cards.subject: An imperative script
says: lists the exact steps to run in order
can fail halfway and leave a partly changed system
cards.use: need a quick one-off sequence of commands
not: describes only the desired end state

cards.subject: Idempotence
says: means applying the same operation twice gives the same result as once
makes it safe to rerun a failed provisioning step
cards.use: need a setup step that is safe to retry after a failure
not: means an operation can be run only one time

cards.subject: A state file
says: records what the infrastructure tool believes it has created
is compared with the code and reality to compute a plan
cards.use: share infrastructure code across a team and need one source of truth about what exists
not: should be edited by hand to speed up changes

cards.subject: A dry-run plan
says: shows the changes a tool would make without making them
lets a reviewer catch an unintended destroy before it happens
cards.use: want to see what a change will delete before approving it
not: applies the changes first and reports afterwards

cards.subject: Immutable infrastructure
says: replaces servers with new ones from a fresh image instead of patching them in place
avoids servers that differ through accumulated manual changes
cards.use: want every server to be a known image so rollback means swapping back
not: patches each live server by hand over time

cards.subject: A snowflake server
says: is a machine whose setup cannot be reproduced because it grew through manual changes
is hard to rebuild after a failure
cards.use: inherit a server nobody dares to touch or rebuild
not: is built from a version-controlled definition

cards.subject: Drift detection
says: compares live infrastructure with its code definition to find manual changes
flags resources changed outside the pipeline
cards.use: suspect someone edited a production setting by hand in a console
not: rebuilds every server on a schedule

cards.subject: Logging
says: records timestamped events as the app runs
gives the detail needed to reconstruct what happened around a failure
cards.use: need to see what the app did just before it failed
not: gives a single number sampled over time for dashboards

cards.subject: A metric
says: is a numeric measurement sampled over time
is cheap to store and suits dashboards and alert thresholds
cards.use: want a graph of requests per second over the last week
not: records the full text of each individual request

cards.subject: A trace
says: follows one request across every service it touches
shows which hop in a chain added the latency
cards.use: need to find which of five services made one request slow
not: counts total errors per minute for the whole system

cards.subject: Structured logging
says: writes log entries as key-value fields such as JSON
lets tools filter on fields instead of searching free text
cards.use: need to find every event with a given request id
not: prints only unformatted free text for humans to read

cards.subject: Observability
says: is how well you can explain internal behavior from the outputs a system emits
lets you ask new questions without shipping new code
cards.use: need to debug an unexpected failure that nobody wrote an alert for
not: is just another word for owning a dashboard

cards.subject: Monitoring
says: watches known indicators and tells you when they cross a threshold
answers questions you thought to ask in advance
cards.use: want to know when a known indicator such as error rate goes past a limit
not: lets you explore failures nobody anticipated without new instrumentation

cards.subject: A health endpoint
says: exposes a URL that reports whether the app is up
is what a deploy script or load balancer polls
cards.use: want a deploy script to confirm the app came back
not: proves every feature works for every user

cards.subject: Synthetic monitoring
says: sends scripted requests to the live service on a schedule
can detect an outage when no real user is online
cards.use: want to know the login page is down at 3 a.m. before a customer tells you
not: waits for real users to report problems

cards.subject: An alert
says: notifies a person when a condition needs action
should be actionable and point to a next step
cards.use: need a person woken only when something needs doing
not: should fire on every metric that moves

cards.subject: Alert fatigue
says: happens when frequent low-value alerts train people to ignore them
is reduced by alerting on symptoms users feel and removing noisy rules
cards.use: notice the team muting the pager channel because it fires constantly
not: is cured by adding more alerts for every metric

cards.subject: The golden-signals method
says: covers latency, traffic, errors and saturation
gives a short starting list of what to watch for any service
cards.use: are asked what to monitor first on a service you have never seen
not: covers only CPU, memory, disk and network

cards.subject: Metric cardinality
says: grows with the number of distinct label combinations on a metric
explodes when labels hold unbounded values such as user ids
cards.use: see a metrics bill or database balloon after adding a user id label
not: is the number of dashboards a team may create

cards.subject: A service level indicator
says: is a measured quantity describing service behavior, such as the share of successful requests
is the raw measurement an SLO sets a target on
cards.use: need a precise number for how well the service is doing
not: is the contract that refunds customers when missed

cards.subject: A service level objective
says: is an internal target for an indicator over a period, such as 99.9 percent of requests succeeding in 30 days
guides how much reliability work is worth doing
cards.use: need an agreed target to decide when reliability is good enough
not: is a legal promise that refunds customers when missed

cards.subject: A service level agreement
says: is a contractual promise to customers with consequences if missed
is usually looser than the internal objective behind it
cards.use: need to know what the customer contract guarantees and what happens on a breach
not: is a purely internal target with no contractual weight

cards.subject: An error budget
says: is the amount of unreliability an SLO allows over its period
shifts effort from new features to reliability when it is spent
cards.use: need an objective way to decide whether to ship risky changes or stabilise
not: is money set aside to compensate customers after an outage

cards.subject: Availability
says: is the share of time or requests in which a service works
is often quoted as a number of nines
cards.use: are asked what percentage of the time users could use the service
not: measures how fast the service responds

cards.subject: Tail latency
says: is the response time that, for p99, 99 percent of requests beat
exposes slow outliers that an average hides
cards.use: see a healthy average response time yet users still complain of slowness
not: is identical to the mean response time

cards.subject: A single point of failure
says: is a component whose failure takes the whole service down
is removed by adding redundancy
cards.use: ask what happens if this one server dies
not: is any component that has more than one copy

cards.subject: Graceful degradation
says: keeps core functions working while optional features switch off under failure
serves a reduced experience instead of an error page
cards.use: must keep checkout working while a recommendations service is down
not: fails the whole page whenever any dependency fails

cards.subject: Retry with backoff
says: retries a failed call after growing, jittered delays
prevents a recovering service being flattened by synchronised retries
cards.use: see a briefly failing dependency hammered by callers that all retry at once
not: retries instantly and forever to guarantee success

cards.subject: A circuit breaker
says: stops calling a failing dependency for a while after repeated errors
fails fast so a slow dependency does not exhaust the caller's threads
cards.use: see calls piling up behind a downstream service that is timing out
not: retries every failed call until it succeeds

cards.subject: A secrets manager
says: stores secrets encrypted and hands them to authorised workloads at runtime
keeps an audit trail of who read each secret
cards.use: want credentials out of code and out of config files on disk
not: is a file committed to the repository for convenience

cards.subject: Secret rotation
says: replaces a credential with a new one on a schedule or after exposure
limits how long a stolen credential stays useful
cards.use: want a stolen key to stop working without anyone noticing the theft
not: keeps the same credential forever so nothing breaks

cards.subject: Least privilege
says: gives an identity only the permissions its job needs
limits the damage a compromised account can do
cards.use: set up a deploy account that only needs to restart one app
not: gives every engineer admin rights to avoid blocking them

cards.subject: Secret scanning
says: searches commits and repositories for accidentally committed credentials
can block a push that contains a key
cards.use: worry that someone pasted an API key into code
not: checks third-party packages for known vulnerabilities

cards.subject: Dependency scanning
says: checks third-party packages against databases of known vulnerabilities
flags a vulnerable package even when your own code is unchanged
cards.use: want warning when a library you use gets a security advisory
not: searches your commits for pasted passwords

cards.subject: Static application security testing
says: inspects your own source for insecure patterns without running it
finds issues such as injection-prone code before deployment
cards.use: want insecure coding patterns caught during code review
not: lists known-vulnerable versions of libraries you installed

cards.subject: A software bill of materials
says: lists every component and version inside a software build
lets you find which products contain a newly disclosed vulnerable library
cards.use: must find where a newly announced vulnerable library ships
not: encrypts the artifact so it cannot be altered

cards.subject: Short-lived credentials
says: expire automatically after minutes or hours
reduce the value of a token leaked from a pipeline
cards.use: want a pipeline token that is useless soon after it leaks
not: are issued once and stay valid for years

cards.subject: A leaked secret
says: must be revoked and rotated even after it is deleted from git history
should be assumed copied by anyone who could read the repository
cards.use: find an API key in a public commit
not: is fixed by deleting the commit and carrying on

cards.subject: Deployment frequency
says: counts how often a team releases to production
rises when changes are small and releases are routine
cards.use: want to know how often we ship
not: measures how long a change takes from commit to production

cards.subject: Lead time for changes
says: measures the time from a commit to running in production
is shortened by small batches and automated pipelines
cards.use: want to know how long an idea takes to reach users once coded
not: counts how many releases happen in a week

cards.subject: Change failure rate
says: is the share of deployments that cause a failure needing a fix or rollback
tracks the quality side of delivery speed
cards.use: want to know whether shipping faster is breaking things
not: is the number of bugs found in code review

cards.subject: Time to restore service
says: measures how long it takes to recover after a production failure
is improved by fast rollback and good alerting
cards.use: want to know how quickly the team recovers when a release goes wrong
not: counts how many incidents happen per month

cards.subject: Mean time to detect
says: is the time from a failure starting to someone knowing about it
is shortened by symptom-based alerting and synthetic checks
cards.use: find out about outages from customers rather than from your own alerts
not: is the time it takes to finish writing the postmortem

cards.subject: Batch size
says: is the amount of change released together
shrinks risk and speeds feedback when it is reduced
cards.use: releases keep breaking and each one contains weeks of changes
not: is safest when many weeks of changes ship together

cards.subject: Goodhart's law
says: says a measure stops being a good measure once it becomes a target
warns that rewarding deploy counts can encourage splitting changes pointlessly
cards.use: managers want to rank teams by deployment frequency
not: says a metric becomes more accurate once teams are rewarded for it

cards.subject: An on-call rotation
says: shares responsibility for responding to alerts among a team in turns
gives one named person ownership at any moment
cards.use: need someone accountable to answer alerts out of hours
not: makes every engineer respond to every alert at once

cards.subject: A runbook
says: documents the steps to diagnose and fix a known problem
lets a tired responder act without recalling details
cards.use: get paged for a known failure at night and want the fix steps written down
not: records why the team chose an architecture

cards.subject: An escalation policy
says: defines who is paged next if the first responder does not acknowledge
prevents an alert dying because one person missed it
cards.use: want an unacknowledged page to reach someone else automatically
not: lists the steps for fixing a particular fault

cards.subject: A severity level
says: classifies an incident by its user impact
decides how fast and how widely people are mobilised
cards.use: need to decide whether an issue wakes the whole team or can wait until morning
not: names the engineer responsible for the outage

cards.subject: An incident commander
says: coordinates the response and decisions during an incident
does not usually do the hands-on fixing themselves
cards.use: run an incident with many people where nobody knows who decides
not: writes the postmortem alone after the incident

cards.subject: A blameless postmortem
says: reviews an incident to find causes and improvements rather than someone to blame
ends with tracked follow-up actions
cards.use: want to learn from an outage that is now over
not: names the engineer at fault so they can be disciplined

cards.subject: A status page
says: tells users what is broken and when to expect an update
reduces support load during an outage
cards.use: want customers to see an outage acknowledged without emailing support
not: is where engineers keep their internal runbooks

cards.subject: Toil
says: is repetitive manual operational work that grows with the service and could be automated
signals a task worth automating
cards.use: keep manually restarting the same service every week
not: is the creative design work done during incidents

cards.subject: A game day
says: rehearses a failure on purpose to test systems and responders
finds gaps in runbooks before a real incident
cards.use: want to learn whether the team and tooling cope with a database failure before it happens for real
not: is the scheduled day for deploying the quarterly release

cards.subject: The GGLearn deploy script
says: rsyncs the code to the server and then runs the remote steps
sets -euo pipefail so any failing step stops it
cards.use: need to ship GGLearn to the server
not: relies on a hosted CI service to run each deploy

cards.subject: The GGLearn rsync exclude list
says: leaves node_modules, .next, .git, the SQLite database files and every .env file off the sync
stops a deploy overwriting production secrets or data
cards.use: worry that a deploy might overwrite production secrets or the database
not: includes the .env files so production gets the right secrets

cards.subject: Streaming the remote steps into bash
says: feeds the remote steps to bash instead of the server's login shell
exists because the server's login shell is fish, which cannot parse bash syntax
cards.use: ask why the remote steps are not simply run in the server's default shell
not: is needed because the server has no shell at all

cards.subject: The flock lock
says: stops two deploys running on the server at the same time
is taken at the start of the remote steps
cards.use: worry that two people might deploy at the same moment
not: encrypts the deploy so nobody else can read it

cards.subject: The npm ci step
says: installs exact dependency versions from the lockfile on the server
is the dependency step of the remote deploy
cards.use: ask how GGLearn gets repeatable dependencies on the server
not: upgrades every package to its latest version

cards.subject: The drizzle-kit push step
says: applies the schema defined in code to the database during deploy
brings the database structure in line with the new release
cards.use: need the database tables to match the new release
not: builds the Next.js production bundle

cards.subject: The pm2 startOrRestart step
says: starts the app if it is not running and restarts it if it is
comes after the build and before the final health check
cards.use: ask how a deploy works for both a first start and a later release
not: only ever starts the app and fails if it is already running

cards.subject: The post-deploy health check
says: polls the app on 127.0.0.1 port 3400 up to ten times
fails the deploy unless it receives HTTP 200
prints recent PM2 error logs when it fails
cards.use: ask how GGLearn knows the app really came back after a deploy
not: only checks that the rsync step exited with status zero

cards.subject: The GGLearn ecosystem.config.cjs
says: defines one app, gglearn-web, running next start on port 3400
sets NODE_ENV to production
cards.use: ask where GGLearn's PM2 process is defined
not: defines separate web and scheduler processes

cards.subject: The max_memory_restart setting
says: is set to 400M for gglearn-web
restarts the process when memory grows past the limit, as a safety net against leaks
cards.use: ask what protects GGLearn's server from a slow memory leak
not: caps the size of the SQLite database at 400 MB

cards.subject: Apache in front of GGLearn
says: is the only thing that reaches the app, which listens on 127.0.0.1 port 3400
is why the Next.js server is started bound to localhost
cards.use: ask why GGLearn is not directly exposed on its port
not: connects to the app over the public internet address

cards.subject: The GGLearn in-memory rate limiter
says: assumes a single process
would break with several PM2 instances unless its state moved to the database
cards.use: are asked to run three PM2 instances of GGLearn for more capacity
not: is stored in the database and works across any number of instances

cards.subject: The DATABASE_FILE variable
says: sets the path of GGLearn's SQLite database
has a default under data/ for local use
cards.use: need to point GGLearn at a different database file
not: selects between Postgres and MySQL

cards.subject: The GGLearn README's database advice
says: says SQLite suits local development
suggests Postgres before heavier multi-user production use
cards.use: ask whether SQLite is the long-term plan for heavy production use
not: recommends SQLite for any amount of production traffic

cards.subject: The ggsocial pre-flight checks
says: run type-check, lint and tests before shipping
stop a broken change reaching the server
cards.use: ask what ggsocial verifies before it deploys
not: run only after the new build is already live

cards.subject: The ggsocial database backup
says: is taken before changes are applied
gives a way back if a change damages data
cards.use: ask what ggsocial does to protect data before a deploy
not: is taken only after the deploy succeeded

cards.subject: The ggsocial build swap
says: builds into a fresh directory and then swaps it in
lets the old build keep serving until the new one is ready
cards.use: ask how ggsocial avoids downtime while building
not: builds in place over the files that are serving traffic

cards.subject: The ggsocial .env guard
says: stops the deploy if .env is missing
exists because rsync --delete without an exclude could delete the production secrets
cards.use: ask why ggsocial's deploy script refuses to continue without a .env file
not: creates a new random .env file when none exists

cards.subject: The ggsocial APP_SECRET
says: logs every user out when it is lost
makes stored platform tokens unreadable when it is lost
cards.use: ask why losing one value in ggsocial's production config is serious
not: can be regenerated at any time with no effect on users

cards.subject: The ggsocial database container
says: runs the database in a container on 127.0.0.1
keeps its data in a named volume
cards.use: ask which part of ggsocial runs in a container
not: also containerises the ggsocial web app

cards.subject: The ggsocial scheduler
says: runs as its own PM2 process
follows the one-concern-per-process rule
cards.use: ask why ggsocial's scheduled jobs are not inside the web process
not: runs inside the web process to share its memory

cards.subject: The tick failed message
says: is logged once by the ggsocial scheduler during every restart
is expected once but not when it keeps repeating
cards.use: see 'tick failed: fetch failed' once in the logs right after a restart
not: proves the deploy failed and must be rolled back

cards.subject: The ggmoney APP_ENV
says: is either sandbox or production
makes a sandbox install refuse to email real employees
cards.use: ask how ggmoney avoids emailing real employees from a test install
not: makes a sandbox install email employees twice to test delivery

cards.subject: The ggmoney config.local.php
says: is kept out of the upload so a deploy never overwrites it
holds environment-specific settings outside the shipped code
cards.use: ask how ggmoney keeps environment settings out of its deploys
not: is committed to the repository with the production values

cards.subject: The ggmoney bin/alerts.php
says: runs from cron on weekday mornings
emails owners what needs attention, such as deadlines
sends nothing when there is nothing to report
cards.use: ask how ggmoney reminds owners of deadlines without nagging
not: emails every owner a daily digest even when empty

cards.subject: The ggmoney deploy-check.php
says: reports whether the rules are really in force
is a separate script from the cron alerts job
cards.use: ask how ggmoney confirms its rules are actually enforced
not: emails owners about upcoming deadlines

qa.q: Why is .env listed in .gitignore?
qa.right: So local secrets are not committed to the repository
wrong: So Git can compress the file better
So the file is deployed twice
So the app ignores the file at runtime
qa.why: A gitignored file is never staged by default, which keeps credentials out of version control.

qa.q: What happens when npm ci fails on the server in this script?
qa.right: The script exits with an error and never prints deployed
wrong: The script prints deployed anyway because ssh succeeded
Only a warning is shown and the rsync is reversed
The script retries npm ci forever
qa.why: set -e (with -u and pipefail) stops the script on the first failing command, and ssh returns the remote command's exit status.
qa.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
rsync -az ./ server:/app/
ssh server "cd /app && npm ci && npm run build"
echo "deployed"

qa.q: With pipefail set, what does this print?
wrong: true
qa.why: pipefail makes a pipeline return the status of the last command that failed, here false.

qa.q: What does the -n option do in this command?
qa.right: Fails immediately with busy if another process holds the lock, instead of waiting
wrong: Encrypts the lock file
Runs the script in the background
Deletes the lock file after use
qa.why: flock -n is non-blocking: it gives up at once when the lock is taken.

qa.q: What does this loop accomplish?
qa.right: It retries up to ten times and fails the deploy if the app never returns 200
wrong: It restarts the app ten times in a row
It sends ten emails to the team
It deletes old builds until one returns 200
qa.why: A post-deploy check should verify the app really came back and fail the deploy if it did not.
qa.code:
for i in $(seq 1 10); do
  code=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://127.0.0.1:3400/)
  [ "$code" = "200" ] && exit 0
  sleep 2
done
exit 1

qa.q: What happens when this process passes 400 MB of memory?
qa.right: The process manager restarts it
wrong: The process is paused until memory frees up
The database is truncated
The deploy is rolled back
qa.why: max_memory_restart tells PM2 to restart a process that exceeds the limit, a safety net against leaks.

qa.q: What does this command do when the app is not yet running?
qa.right: It starts the app from the ecosystem file
wrong: It fails because nothing is running
It only restarts apps that are already running
It deletes the ecosystem file
qa.why: startOrRestart works for both a first start and a later restart.

qa.q: Which command lists the processes PM2 is managing?
qa.right: pm2 list
wrong: pm2 show-all
pm2 processes
pm2 inspect --all
qa.why: pm2 list (alias ls) prints the managed processes and their status.

qa.q: Why does this Dockerfile copy package*.json and run npm ci before COPY . .?
qa.right: So the dependency layer is cached and reused when only source files change
wrong: So npm ci can see the source files
Because Docker forbids copying the source first
To make the final image smaller than any other order
qa.why: Docker caches layers in order; an unchanged package file keeps the expensive install layer cached.
qa.code:
FROM node:lts-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
CMD ["npm", "start"]

qa.q: What does the -p 127.0.0.1:5432:5432 part do?
qa.right: Publishes the container port only on the host's loopback address
wrong: Opens the database to the whole internet
Maps host port 127 to container port 5432
Blocks all connections to the container
qa.why: Prefixing the host IP limits the published port to that interface; 127.0.0.1 is local only.

qa.q: After docker rm of that container, what happens to the data in the pgdata volume?
qa.right: It remains in the volume and can be mounted by a new container
wrong: It is deleted with the container
It is moved into the image
It is uploaded to the registry
qa.why: Named volumes outlive containers; only removing the volume deletes the data.
qa.code:
docker rm -f db
docker volume ls

qa.q: What does this command do?
qa.right: Creates an annotated tag marking the current commit as the release
wrong: Deletes the v1.4.0 branch
Pushes the release to production
Renames the latest commit
qa.why: A tag records the exact commit a release was built from.

qa.q: A fix is on main as commit abc123 and only the release/2.1 branch needs it. Which commands apply it?
qa.right: git switch release/2.1 then git cherry-pick abc123
wrong: git switch release/2.1 then git merge main
git rebase release/2.1 on main
git reset --hard abc123 on release/2.1
qa.why: Cherry-pick applies one commit without bringing along the rest of main's work.
qa.code:
git switch release/2.1
git cherry-pick abc123

qa.q: The current version is 2.3.1 and a release removes a parameter from a public API. What should the next version be?
qa.why: Backwards-incompatible changes bump the major version.

qa.q: The current version is 2.3.1 and a release adds a backwards-compatible feature. What should the next version be?
qa.why: New compatible functionality bumps the minor version and resets the patch.

qa.q: What does needs: test do in this pipeline?
qa.right: The deploy job waits for the test job and runs only if it succeeds
wrong: The deploy job runs first and test follows
Both jobs run in parallel with no order
The test job is skipped when deploy is present
qa.why: A needs relationship expresses job dependency, forming a gate.
qa.code:
jobs:
  test:
    steps:
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
  deploy:
    needs: test
    steps:
      - run: ./deploy.sh

qa.q: Roughly what share of requests reaches the second server here?
qa.right: About 10 percent
wrong: About 50 percent
About 1 percent
All requests until the first fails
qa.why: Weights 9 and 1 split traffic roughly 90/10, a simple canary.

qa.q: What does this Apache configuration do?
qa.right: Forwards public requests to an app listening on the local machine
wrong: Redirects visitors to a different domain
Serves static files from port 3400
Blocks requests to port 3400
qa.why: ProxyPass makes Apache act as a reverse proxy to the backend; ProxyPassReverse rewrites response headers.

qa.q: How much downtime does a 99.9 percent availability SLO allow in a 30-day month?
qa.right: About 43 minutes
wrong: About 4 minutes
About 7 hours
About 43 seconds
qa.why: 30 days is 43,200 minutes and 0.1 percent of that is about 43.

qa.q: How much downtime does 99.99 percent availability allow in a 30-day month?
qa.right: About 4.3 minutes
wrong: About 43 minutes
About 26 seconds
About 4 hours
qa.why: 0.01 percent of 43,200 minutes is about 4.3 minutes.

qa.q: A 99.9 percent monthly SLO has used 40 of its 43 error-budget minutes by day 12, and a risky migration is planned. What should the team do?
qa.right: Slow down risky changes and prioritise reliability work until the budget recovers
wrong: Ship the migration because the SLA is not yet breached
Raise the SLO target so the budget is larger
Delete the alert that reported the downtime
qa.why: A nearly spent error budget is the signal to trade feature risk for stability.

qa.q: An alert fires nightly when CPU passes 80 percent for one minute and nobody ever acts on it. What is the best fix?
qa.right: Remove or retune it and alert on a user-visible symptom instead
wrong: Page more people so it gets noticed
Lower the threshold to 60 percent
Mute the pager channel permanently
qa.why: Alerts nobody acts on cause fatigue; alert on symptoms that need action.

qa.q: Average latency is 120 ms but p99 is 4 s. What does this suggest?
qa.right: A small share of requests is very slow, so the tail needs investigating
wrong: The service is healthy because the average is low
The p99 figure must be a measurement error
Every request takes about 4 seconds
qa.why: Averages hide outliers; percentiles reveal them.

qa.q: Why is the second form of this log line more useful than a free-text message?
qa.right: Tools can filter and aggregate on its fields such as order_id
wrong: It uses fewer characters than free text
It cannot contain errors
It is never written to disk
qa.why: Key-value fields make logs searchable and countable.

qa.q: What is the problem with this metric?
qa.right: The user_id label has unbounded values and creates a huge number of time series
wrong: Counters cannot have labels
The name must end in _seconds
Status codes must not be labels
qa.why: Each distinct label combination is its own series; unbounded labels cause a cardinality explosion.

qa.q: What is the random term for in this retry delay?
qa.right: It adds jitter so many clients do not retry at the same moment
wrong: It makes the delay shorter on every attempt
It ensures the request succeeds
It chooses which server to call
qa.why: Jitter spreads retries out and avoids a synchronised wave.

qa.q: A developer committed an API key to a public repository and deleted it in the next commit. What should happen first?
qa.right: Revoke and rotate the key, because it must be assumed copied
wrong: Nothing, since the new commit removed it
Wait for the next release to remove the history
Rename the repository
qa.why: A secret in public history is compromised the moment it is pushed.

qa.q: What does --exclude .env achieve in this command?
qa.right: It stops the server's .env from being overwritten or deleted by --delete
wrong: It deletes .env on the server
It encrypts .env during transfer
It copies .env twice for safety
qa.why: Excluded paths are neither transferred nor removed unless --delete-excluded is used.

qa.q: The server has a .env that is not in the local project. What does this command do to it?
qa.right: It deletes it because --delete removes files missing from the source
wrong: It keeps it because dotfiles are always protected
It overwrites it with an empty file
It moves it to a backup folder
qa.why: Without an exclude rule, --delete removes extra files at the destination.

qa.q: You must rename the column email to contact_email during a rolling deploy with no downtime. What is the safe approach?
qa.right: Add the new column, write both, backfill, switch reads, and drop the old column in a later release
wrong: Rename the column in the same release as the code change
Stop all traffic, rename, then restart
Drop email first and recreate it as contact_email
qa.why: Expand and contract keeps old and new app versions working against the same schema.

qa.q: A release changed data in a way the old version cannot read, and users report errors. What is usually safest?
qa.right: Roll forward with a corrected release
wrong: Roll back to the previous version immediately
Restore last week's backup over production
Switch off monitoring until it settles
qa.why: Rolling back to code that cannot read the new data can make things worse.

qa.q: A deploy script exited 0, yet the site returns 502. What was missing from the pipeline?
qa.right: A post-deploy health check that fails the deploy when the app does not respond
wrong: A longer rsync timeout
A second copy of the lockfile
More verbose build logs
qa.why: Steps can succeed while the app still fails to start; verify the result.

qa.q: Two teammates ran the deploy at the same moment and the build was corrupted. What prevents this?
qa.right: A lock such as flock around the remote steps
wrong: A faster network connection
Running npm install instead of npm ci
Disabling the health check
qa.why: A lock serialises deploys so one finishes before the next starts.

qa.q: Staging passes but production fails; staging uses a different database engine. What principle was violated?
qa.right: Environment parity
wrong: Least privilege
Semantic versioning
Error budgeting
qa.why: Differences between environments hide bugs until production.

qa.q: A test fails one run in ten and the team re-runs until green. What is the best response?
qa.right: Quarantine it, find the root cause and fix or delete it
wrong: Keep re-running until it passes
Raise the pass threshold to 90 percent
Disable all tests in that suite
qa.why: Flaky tests erode trust in the pipeline and should be fixed or removed.

qa.q: A team doubled deployment frequency and change failure rate rose from 5 to 25 percent. What does this suggest?
qa.right: Speed has been gained at the cost of quality, so look at test coverage and validation
wrong: The DORA metrics are unrelated to each other
The team should deploy even more often
Failures are caused only by monitoring
qa.why: Throughput and stability should improve together; diverging figures signal a problem.

qa.q: A server restarts every six hours because of max_memory_restart, and users see occasional errors. What should you do first?
qa.right: Investigate the leak and restart gracefully, keeping the limit as a safety net
wrong: Raise the limit to a very large value
Remove the limit so the process is never killed
Add more servers and ignore the leak
qa.why: The limit hides a symptom; find the leak and avoid dropping in-flight requests.

qa.q: Two instances sit behind a proxy and users are logged out at random because sessions live in each process's memory. What is the fix?
qa.right: Move session state to a shared store
wrong: Turn off the proxy
Run the instances on different ports only
Shorten the session cookie
qa.why: In-memory state is per process; shared state must live somewhere common.

qa.q: A Postgres container was recreated from a new image and all data vanished. What was probably missing?
qa.right: A volume mounted at the data directory
wrong: A larger memory limit
A reverse proxy
A health endpoint
qa.why: Container filesystems are disposable; data needs a volume.

qa.q: Which strategy needs capacity for two full environments at once?
qa.right: Blue/green deployment
wrong: Rolling deployment
Recreate deployment
Canary at one percent
qa.why: Blue/green runs old and new fully in parallel.

qa.q: A canary at 5 percent shows an error rate equal to baseline but p99 latency up 30 percent. What should you do?
qa.right: Hold or abort promotion and investigate the latency
wrong: Promote to 100 percent because errors are unchanged
Ignore latency because users rarely notice it
Restart the canary until latency drops
qa.why: Error rate alone is not enough; slowdowns are also failures.

qa.q: A liveness probe queries the database; the database blips for a minute and every instance restarts at once. What is the lesson?
qa.right: Liveness should check only the process itself, not its dependencies
wrong: Probes should never be used
The restart interval was too long
Use a bigger database
qa.why: Dependency failures should affect readiness at most, not trigger mass restarts.

qa.q: An infrastructure plan shows destroy then create for a database after you renamed its resource in code. What should you do?
qa.right: Stop and move or rename the resource in state instead of applying
wrong: Apply it because the plan is automatic
Approve it and restore from backup afterwards
Delete the state file and run again
qa.why: A rename in code can look like destroy and create; review the plan before applying.

qa.q: Which command previews infrastructure changes in Terraform without applying them?
qa.right: terraform plan
wrong: terraform preview
terraform apply -dry
terraform check
qa.why: plan computes and shows the changes without making them.

qa.q: Why tag container images with versions rather than only latest?
qa.right: So you can reproduce a release and roll back to a known image
wrong: Because latest is not allowed
To make images smaller
To skip pushing to the registry
qa.why: A moving tag cannot tell you what is running or what to return to.
qa.code:
docker build -t app:1.4.2 .
docker push app:1.4.2

qa.q: Why should an internal SLO be tighter than the customer SLA?
qa.right: So the team reacts before the contractual promise is breached
wrong: So customers receive larger refunds
Because SLOs are legally binding
To remove the need for monitoring
qa.why: The gap gives time to act before a contractual breach.

qa.q: Management sets a target of 20 deploys per team per week and teams start splitting changes into trivial pieces. Which idea explains this?
qa.right: Goodhart's law
wrong: Amdahl's law
The CAP theorem
Conway's law
qa.why: When a measure becomes a target, people optimise the number rather than the outcome.

qa.q: A draft postmortem says the outage was caused by Sam running the wrong command. What is the better framing?
qa.right: Ask why the system allowed the command and add a guardrail
wrong: Keep the blame to deter repeats
Remove the section on causes
Restrict Sam's access without investigation
qa.why: Blameless reviews fix conditions, not individuals.

qa.q: A feature flag for a launched feature has been on for everyone for a year. What should you do?
qa.right: Remove the flag and dead code path
wrong: Keep it forever as insurance
Rename the flag
Turn it off to test it
qa.why: Stale flags add branches and risk and should be cleaned up.

qa.q: A CI log shows a pasted API key from echo $API_KEY. What is the right response?
qa.right: Rotate the key and mask secrets in pipeline output
wrong: Delete the log line and continue
Shorten the log retention
Rename the variable
qa.why: Anything printed to logs must be treated as exposed.

qa.q: npm ci fails with a message that package.json and package-lock.json are not in sync. What is the usual fix?
qa.right: Run npm install locally and commit the updated lockfile
wrong: Delete package.json
Run npm ci with --force on the server
Skip the install step
qa.why: npm ci refuses to modify the lockfile, so it must be corrected and committed.

qa.q: Unfinished work must merge to main daily without reaching users. What is the usual technique?
qa.right: Hide it behind a feature flag that is off by default
wrong: Keep it on a branch for a month
Commit it to a release branch only
Skip code review
qa.why: Flags separate merging from releasing.

qa.q: What time does this crontab entry run?
qa.right: 08:00 from Monday to Friday
wrong: 08:00 every day
00:08 every weekday
Eight times a day on weekdays
qa.why: Fields are minute, hour, day-of-month, month, day-of-week; 1-5 means Monday to Friday.

qa.q: What does this command print?
qa.right: The HTTP status code of the response
wrong: The page body
The response time in seconds
The server's IP address
qa.why: -w with %{http_code} prints the status code and -o /dev/null discards the body.

qa.q: An ops team restarts the same service by hand every week. Which concept describes this and what should it do?
qa.right: Toil, so automate it or fix the cause
wrong: A game day, so repeat it monthly
A runbook, so leave it manual
An error budget, so stop it
qa.why: Repetitive manual work that scales with the service should be automated away.
